proposal.title: Add June 1979 Apple II and S-100 portability profiles
proposal.reason: Accepted source-level compatibility design: extend existing standards with dated native Apple output and ROM-backed TUI profiles. IDE 2.0 is a product release, not a new TUI standard. Preserve the 1978 baseline and 1980/1982 chronology; native Apple hardware functions remain separate from portable Logix APIs.

specification.chapter_name: Scope, chronology and compatibility
specification.description: The Z80/enhanced-CP/M developer environment launches on 6 June 1978. ERA/AIONix exploratory work begins on 1 February 1978, but its commercial developer environment belongs to the Artemis launch on 19 May 1980. These are coexisting target profiles of one source-portability contract, not successive standard versions. The platform API is explicitly labelled 1.0; this is not evidence that every module or later operating system has the same release number. Each target retains its own compiler, libraries, ABI and resource constraints. Optional graphics capabilities must be queried. Networking belongs to the 1981 programme; mouse/professional graphics integration belongs to the 1982 programme. Athena/AIONix2 compatibility is a later planning/qualification commitment, not a released capability of the original standard. A new contract revision requires a documented semantic or compatibility change; no new revision numbers are invented.

specification.chapter_name: Source portability and build profiles — Source portability and shared contracts
specification.description:
Cross-platform family overview. Z80/CP/M availability is June 1978; ERA/AIONix availability is May 1980. Later-host features do not become available on earlier computers through source portability alone.

The framework targets {Targets}. Applications share source code, libraries and API meanings; moving between instruction sets still requires a target-specific build.

Recompile shared application code with the target compiler and target libraries. Adapt OS-specific modules, resource budgets and assembly; binary compatibility is a separate CP/M-80 module path.

The framework aims to show third-party developers that moving from the 8-bit platform to Artemis is comparatively easy.

Its portability mechanisms are {Mechanisms}. Shared contracts are defined in {Shared contract references}.

specification.chapter_name: Source portability and build profiles — Limits of portability
specification.description:
Cross-platform family overview. Z80/CP/M availability is June 1978; ERA/AIONix availability is May 1980. Later-host features do not become available on earlier computers through source portability alone.

Portability work must address instruction sets, OS interfaces, memory ownership and file encoding. More capable hardware does not automatically make its application features available on an older host.

Single foreground versus multiple processes: explicit context ownership and shared-service synchronization.

Instruction set: recompile C and replace assembly.

CP/M record/drive interfaces versus AIONix streams, paths and descriptors: use file adapters.

Banked versus virtual memory: use object handles and bounded buffers.

Disk structures: serialize portable fields rather than dumping C objects.

More RAM and a wider display do not make later Artemis-only features available on Aurelia.

specification.chapter_name: Language and target profiles — ABI and conformance responsibilities
specification.description:

specification.chapter_name: Apple II target profile — June 1979
specification.description: The {target} target generates native MOS 6502 code from the documented contemporary C subset. The compiler and IDE execute on Aurelia under enhanced CP/M; the output executes on Apple II without CP/M or a Z80 coprocessor. The target uses 8-bit char, 16-bit short/int/data pointers and 32-bit long, with target-specific calling conventions and software arithmetic helpers. Define signedness, layout, zero-page allocation and separate hardware-return/software-data stacks. Persistent data uses explicit serialization, not raw structure copies. Z80 assembly and direct platform accesses require target-specific replacements.

specification.chapter_name: Apple II build profiles and hardware libraries
specification.description: The {profiles} profiles separate dependencies. The native profile provides console/file adapters and explicitly Apple-specific text, low/high-resolution graphics, speaker, paddle/button and supported peripheral access; those operations do not require Logix video. specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Native Logix applications use a common command vocabulary. Terminal compatibility profiles remain explicit so an editing shortcut cannot silently become a process-control command.

Native Logix-aware editors, forms, spreadsheets, file views and application lifecycle. Legacy CP/M console and Unix-compatible terminal sessions retain explicitly selected compatibility profiles.

Forward-looking alternative-history design at the TUI launch; later DOS, Windows and Linux conventions are design references, not claimed historical 1978 standards.

Arrows navigate; Ctrl modifies navigation granularity; Shift extends selection using the same movement destination.

Ctrl supplies editing/document commands; Alt supplies menu and system actions. System-reserved commands cannot be rebound by applications.

Dispatch stable logical command identifiers separately from physical keys. Resolve focused control, active dialog, application and system ownership explicitly.

Show shortcuts in menus/help; disabled or unavailable commands report their state. Compatibility profiles are explicit, visible and never silently mixed.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Navigation and selection
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Navigation commands move the caret or selection by a defined unit. Shift extends the same movement; selection clearing respects active menus and dialogs. For example, character movement uses Left / Right.

Use {MOVE_CHARACTER_LEFT / RIGHT} for move character left / right (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_DISPLAY_LINE_UP / DOWN} for move display line up / down (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_WORD_LEFT / RIGHT} for move word left / right (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_LINE_START / END} for move line start / end (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_DOCUMENT_START / END} for move document start / end (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_PAGE_UP / DOWN} for move page up / down (native TUI).

Use {MOVE_PARAGRAPH_PREVIOUS / NEXT} for move paragraph previous / next (native TUI).

Use {EXTEND_SELECTION} for extend selection (native TUI).

Use {SELECT_ALL} for select all (focused editor/view).

Use {CLEAR_SELECTION} for clear selection (only after higher-priority transient UI is dismissed).

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Editing and undo
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Copy, cut, paste and undo have shared logical commands. Keyboard aliases retain the same command scope. Copy uses Ctrl+C; alias Ctrl+Insert, while paste uses Ctrl+V; alias Shift+Insert.

Use {COPY} for copy (native TUI).

Use {CUT} for cut (native TUI).

Use {PASTE} for paste (native TUI).

Use {UNDO} for undo (native TUI).

Use {REDO} for redo (native TUI).

Use {DELETE_PREVIOUS / NEXT_CHARACTER} for delete previous / next character (native TUI).

Use {DELETE_PREVIOUS / NEXT_WORD} for delete previous / next word (native TUI).

parameters.value: Ctrl+X; alias Shift+Delete in text editors only

specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Document commands cover creation, opening, saving, search and closure. Save uses Ctrl+S; the application must still report errors and protect modified work.

Use {NEW_DOCUMENT} for new document (native TUI).

Use {OPEN_DOCUMENT} for open document (native TUI).

Use {SAVE_DOCUMENT} for save document (native TUI).

Use {SAVE_DOCUMENT_AS} for save document as (native TUI).

Use {PRINT_DOCUMENT} for print document (native TUI).

Use {FIND} for find (native TUI).

Use {FIND_NEXT / PREVIOUS} for find next / previous (native TUI).

Use {REPLACE} for replace (native TUI).

Use {GO_TO} for go to (line, cell or record in a document; context named in UI).

Use {CLOSE_DOCUMENT} for close document (native TUI).

Use {QUIT_APPLICATION} for quit application (native TUI).

Use {HELP} for help (native TUI).

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Focus, dialogs and application lifecycle
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Focus and lifecycle commands are dispatched to the appropriate control, dialog, application or system. Cooperative cancellation uses Ctrl+Break; it does not imply forced termination.

Use {FOCUS_NEXT / PREVIOUS_FIELD} for focus next / previous field (forms/dialogs).

Use {ACTIVATE_OR_TOGGLE} for activate or toggle (focused button/checkbox).

Use {ACCEPT_DIALOG} for accept dialog (dialog; editor Enter inserts newline).

Use {CANCEL_CONTEXT} for cancel context (innermost active menu/dialog/transient operation).

Use {OPEN_MENU} for open menu (native TUI).

Use {OPEN_NAMED_MENU} for open named menu (native TUI).

Use {FOCUS_NEXT / PREVIOUS_PANE} for focus next / previous pane (native TUI).

Use {NEXT / PREVIOUS_DOCUMENT} for next / previous document (native TUI).

Use {NEXT / PREVIOUS_APPLICATION} for next / previous application (system).

Use {CLOSE_ACTIVE_SURFACE} for close active surface (system close request with unsaved-work checks).

Use {OPEN_SURFACE_ACTIONS} for open surface actions (system).

Use {REQUEST_CANCEL_OPERATION} for request cancel operation (cooperative cancellation; not immediate forced termination).

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Editing behaviour and ownership of state
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Shared behaviour defines selection boundaries, clipboard failure handling, saving and context-sensitive keys. Resource limits and the single-foreground Aurelia model still apply.

Fixed anchor and moving caret. Plain Left/Right collapses to the corresponding selection edge without an extra step; vertical motion retains the preferred column. Home/End target displayed-line boundaries.

Shared word-boundary implementation groups letters, digits and underscore; freeze punctuation/whitespace traversal in conformance examples. Plain-text paragraphs are separated by blank lines; structured editors use paragraph objects.

Copy/Cut without a selection does nothing. Cut removes data only after clipboard transfer succeeds. Delete preserves clipboard. Typing or pasting replaces a selection as one undoable operation; allocation failure must not partially destroy selected content.

Report Save success only after successful completion; retain modified state on failure. Close offers Save/Discard/Cancel for modified content; Quit checks every modified document.

Spreadsheet navigation selects cells until cell-edit mode, which uses text rules. Editor Tab indents and Shift+Tab unindents; form Tab traverses focus. F6 leaves a multiline editor. Esc acts on only one innermost context per press.

Insertion mode by default. Overwrite is an explicit visibly indicated option; bare Insert does not toggle it by default.

Formatting Ctrl+B/I/U is optional in capable editors. Whole-line deletion, duplication, transpose and rectangular selection remain menu commands outside the common shortcut core.

Aurelia remains single-foreground. Alt+Tab exposes the supported launcher/switch mechanism and does not promise concurrent applications or preserved running state. Query lifecycle capabilities on each host.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Terminal compatibility profiles
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

Terminal sessions may assign control keys to interrupt, suspend or line editing. These are explicit terminal profiles, separate from the native TUI keymap. Terminal copy uses Ctrl+Shift+C.

Native TUI Ctrl+S/Q are Save/Quit and must not be intercepted by software flow control. Terminal sessions may preserve configured XON/XOFF behavior.

Optional WordStar/Emacs profiles are whole opt-in keymaps, not conflicting default aliases. Legacy CP/M control-character semantics are preserved outside native TUI contexts.

Use {INTERRUPT} for interrupt (when terminal processing enables it).

Use {SUSPEND} for suspend (if supported/configured).

Use {EOF_OR_APPLICATION_INPUT} for eof or application input (depends on terminal mode and pending input; not unconditional Quit).

Use {READLINE_LINE_START / END} for readline line start / end (Readline-compatible line editor).

Use {READLINE_DELETE_PREVIOUS_WORD} for readline delete previous word (Readline-compatible line editor).

Use {READLINE_YANK} for readline yank (Readline-compatible line editor).

Use {COPY_TERMINAL_VIEW} for copy terminal view (terminal viewer).

Use {PASTE_TERMINAL} for paste terminal (terminal viewer).

Use {HISTORY_PREVIOUS / NEXT} for history previous / next (supported shell prompt).

Use {HISTORY_REVERSE_SEARCH} for history reverse search (supported shell prompt).

Explicit terminal profile; no selection-dependent change between Ctrl+C Copy and Interrupt.

specification.chapter_name: Keyboard and editing core — Keyboard events and conformance
specification.description:
Native keyboard/editing requirements belong to the TUI core. Terminal and application-lifecycle profiles apply only where the host implements them; later operating-system terminology is design context, not a historical release claim.

The keyboard is {Input contract keyboard reference} and transport uses {Input contract transport reference}. Events must preserve key identity and modifiers; byte-terminal fallbacks must advertise limitations instead of promising ambiguous shortcuts.

Key identity plus Ctrl/Shift/Alt modifier state; text translation is separate. Preserve Ctrl+Shift navigation and Ctrl+Shift letter distinctions.

Traditional byte terminals can conflate Tab/Ctrl+I, Enter/Ctrl+M, Esc/Ctrl+[, Backspace/Ctrl+H and shifted Ctrl letters. Advertise capabilities and offer menu equivalents rather than ambiguous shortcut promises.

Existing keyboard exact layout, event encoding, rollover and firmware remain engineering gates; required controls are conformance requirements, not a qualified new hardware revision.

Input services use {Input contract API reference}. A conforming keyboard provides {Input contract required controls}. The shared input and display contracts are documented in {Related technology references}.

parameters.value: Arrows, Home / End, Page Up / Page Down, Separate Backspace / Delete, Ctrl / Shift / Alt, Function keys, Break

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointer extension — Standard controls and pointer interaction
specification.description:
Optional extension introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Older applications require the qualified service-update or relink path described here; no blanket retrofit is promised.

The mouse extension builds on {Base standard reference} and uses {Device class reference}. Standard controls receive semantic actions while retaining keyboard operation, clipping, capture and modal behaviour.

Hit-test visible enabled standard controls; primary click focuses fields/selects list items and activates buttons/menu actions.

Text widgets support click-to-place caret and drag selection; scrollbar and roller actions respect widget bounds.

Capture drags to their originating context, release on button-up/cancel/removal, respect modal dialogs and clipping.

Vertical roller scrolls the hovered scrollable control, falling back to the focused control; thumb roller similarly scrolls horizontally.

Dispatch existing semantic actions to applications; keyboard shortcuts remain fully functional.

Primary button focuses/selects/activates; secondary opens context actions where provided. Middle-finger roller scrolls vertically; thumb roller scrolls horizontally. Wheels have no implicit press buttons.

parameters.value: the keyboard and control baseline of this TUI standard

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointer extension — Application compatibility and event ownership
specification.description:
Optional extension introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Older applications require the qualified service-update or relink path described here; no blanket retrofit is promised.

Existing applications gain pointer support only through compatible replaceable services or a qualified relink. Input remains owned by the active context, and a hardware cursor consumes an existing sprite resource.

No application source changes for standard controls managed by the TUI library. Existing binaries gain support only when they call replaceable/system TUI services; statically linked copies require relinking with the updated library. Custom drawing, direct console polling and non-TUI applications require explicit adaptation. No blanket mouse retrofit for all CP/M programs.

Aurelia has one foreground application; AIONix routes events only to the appropriate active/context-owned controls, with modal/capture rules and no input leakage.

Library-managed pointer with bounded save/restore on software-rendered targets or optional sprite rendering; application code need not change. A hardware pointer consumes an existing sprite unless separately provisioned; no sixth sprite is implied.

specification.chapter_name: 1982 pointer extension — Mouse and keyboard qualification
specification.description:
Optional extension introduced at NCC on 7 June 1982. Older applications require the qualified service-update or relink path described here; no blanket retrofit is promised.

Test both updated pointer interaction and unchanged keyboard-only use. Rendering, capture, removal and ABI compatibility must work across the supported layouts.

Qualification must cover unchanged standard-control applications.

Qualification must cover static-library relink and ABI conformance.

Qualification must cover text and graphics cursor restore, clipping and scrolling.

Qualification must cover button ordering, drag capture and removal.

Qualification must cover keyboard-only use and 40/80-column layouts.

specification.chapter_name: June 1979 Apple II and S-100 ROM-backed TUI
specification.description: Both Logix video cards provide the same contemporary Aurelia control behaviour, frames, text windows, menus, forms, lists, editing and clipboard semantics, with bounded application state in RAM. ROM primitives and linked composite-control helpers jointly implement the complete profile; application callbacks redraw obscured regions rather than requiring an unbounded window backing store. Apple uses native 6502 firmware and a host runtime. S-100 TUI services require a qualified CP/M installation with the matching TUI/Platform Extensions and an explicitly supported CPU. This requirement concerns supplied TUI services, not the physical ability of the card to display video under another operating system.

specification.chapter_name: Foreign-host input and conformance
specification.description: Preserve logical commands and visible behaviour while mapping host keyboard input. Apple and byte-terminal keyboards may not distinguish the Aurelia modifier combinations; provide unambiguous menu or documented key-sequence equivalents for every command. Exact Aurelia physical shortcuts require a qualified full-event keyboard path, such as the supported FlexiBUS keyboard/interface. Do not interpret missing modifier information as a different command. Test the complete released control set, fonts/frame glyphs, clipping, focus, selection, clipboard, redraw and failure behaviour against Aurelia reference workloads. Screen modes remain subject to the same card/monitor and resource limits; no identical rendering speed or extra host RAM is promised.
